Threads add one more trap. If two threads write to different variables that share a cache line, the line bounces between their caches on every write. The program is correct and slow. This is false sharing, and the cure is to keep each thread's data apart.

lessons.title: How a GPU runs your code
lessons.html:
A processor has a few strong cores. A graphics card has thousands of weak ones that are only good at one thing: running the same small function on many pieces of data at once. CUDA is NVIDIA's way of writing that function in C.

Host and device

The processor and its memory are the host. The graphics card and its memory are the device. They do not share memory. Every GPU program has the same four steps:

  1. copy the data from the host to the device
  2. launch a function on the device
  3. wait for it to finish
  4. copy the results back

Steps 1 and 4 are often slower than step 2. A GPU pays off when a lot of work is done on the data between the two copies.

A kernel runs once per thread

The function is called a kernel. You do not call it in a loop. You launch it, and the device runs it once in each of many threads, all at the same time:

saxpy<<<blocks, threads_per_block>>>(n, a, x, y);

The threads come in blocks of equal size, at most 1024 threads each, and the blocks together form the grid. Blocks exist because the threads of one block can share a small fast memory and wait for each other; threads of different blocks cannot.

Every thread runs the same code, so the first thing a thread does is find out who it is. Four values are there for that:

NameMeaning
threadIdx.xthis thread's number inside its block
blockIdx.xthis block's number inside the grid
blockDim.xthreads per block
gridDim.xblocks in the grid

Each also has .y and .z, for work that is naturally a picture or a volume.

The two lines that start every kernel

int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
if (i < n) ...

The first line turns "thread 5 of block 2" into "element 517". The second is there because the launch rounds up to whole blocks: 1000 elements with 256 threads per block need 4 blocks, which is 1024 threads, and the last 24 have nothing to do. Without the check they write past the end of the array. A GPU gives no error for that. It corrupts whatever was there.

The number of blocks is n divided by the block size, rounded up:

int blocks = (n + threads_per_block - 1) / threads_per_block;

No order is promised

The threads run in whatever order the device likes, and many run at the same instant. Three rules follow, and the exercises are built around them:

  • Each thread writes only its own output. Then the order cannot matter.
  • To read neighbours, read from one array and write to another. Otherwise a thread may see a neighbour before or after its update.
  • Never add into one shared variable. That is the race from the lesson before, a thousand times over. Build sums in rounds, pair by pair, or use an atomic operation such as atomicAdd.

How the exercises model this

The exercises are in Python, so that they run here with no graphics card. One function is already defined for you:

launch(kernel, grid, block, *args)

It calls your kernel once for every thread, in a shuffled order, and passes the thread as the first argument. The names are CUDA's: t.blockIdx.x, t.blockDim.x, t.threadIdx.x, t.gridDim.x. grid and block are pairs, (x, y).

A kernel that is right here is right in CUDA C almost word for word. A kernel that depends on the order the threads run in fails here, as it would on the device.

A complete program in CUDA C

This is the smallest whole program. Type it on a machine with an NVIDIA card, save it as saxpy.cu, and build it with nvcc saxpy.cu -o saxpy.

#include <stdio.h>

__global__ void saxpy(int n, float a, const float *x, float *y) {
    int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    if (i < n) y[i] = a * x[i] + y[i];
}

int main(void) {
    int n = 1 << 20;
    float *x, *y;
    cudaMallocManaged(&x, n * sizeof(float));
    cudaMallocManaged(&y, n * sizeof(float));
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { x[i] = 1.0f; y[i] = 2.0f; }

    saxpy<<<(n + 255) / 256, 256>>>(n, 2.0f, x, y);
    cudaDeviceSynchronize();

    printf("%f\n", y[0]);
    cudaFree(x);
    cudaFree(y);
    return 0;
}

__global__ marks a kernel. cudaMallocManaged asks for memory that both host and device can use, and the system moves it when needed; the older way is cudaMalloc on the device with cudaMemcpy in each direction. cudaDeviceSynchronize waits for the kernel: a launch returns at once, before the work is done. It should print 4.000000.

The same model in Python

Numba compiles a Python function into a real kernel, with the same blocks and threads:

from numba import cuda

@cuda.jit
def saxpy(a, x, y):
    i = cuda.grid(1)
    if i < x.size:
        y[i] = a * x[i] + y[i]

saxpy[blocks, 256](2.0, x, y)

cuda.grid(1) is the index line, done for you.

What PyTorch does with all this

tensor.to("cuda") is the copy to the device. Every operation on a tensor there is a launch of kernels someone else wrote. Two consequences reach you even if you never write a kernel:

  • Launches return before the work is done. To time something on the GPU, call torch.cuda.synchronize() before reading the clock, or you time the launch and not the work.
  • Each launch has a fixed cost. One big batch beats many small ones for that reason, until memory runs out.

What was checked before release: the kernels shown with each exercise, and the complete program above, were compiled as C++ and run on a processor with stand-ins for the CUDA calls. That tests their arithmetic. Nothing was run on a real device, and the Numba lines were not run at all. The Syllabus list under Lists has the programs to write and time on the V100.

lessons.title: MapReduce and message passing
lessons.html:
Threads share one memory. That is convenient and it stops at one machine. To use many machines, each process keeps its own memory, and anything another process needs has to be sent to it.

Message passing

MPI is the standard library for this. You write one program. It is started many times, on one machine or on hundreds, and each copy is told its rank, a number from 0 to size - 1. The copies differ only in what they do with their rank.

#include <mpi.h>
#include <stdio.h>

int main(int argc, char **argv) {
    int rank, size;
    MPI_Init(&argc, &argv);
    MPI_Comm_rank(MPI_COMM_WORLD, &rank);
    MPI_Comm_size(MPI_COMM_WORLD, &size);

    int mine = rank + 1, total = 0;
    MPI_Reduce(&mine, &total, 1, MPI_INT, MPI_SUM, 0, MPI_COMM_WORLD);
    if (rank == 0) printf("%d processes, total %d\n", size, total);

    MPI_Finalize();
    return 0;
}

Build it with mpicc sum.c -o sum and run four copies with mpirun -np 4 ./sum. It prints 4 processes, total 10.

The calls come in two kinds:

  • Point to point. MPI_Send and MPI_Recv move data between two ranks. A plain receive waits until the message arrives, so two ranks that both wait to receive before they send will wait for ever. That is a deadlock.
  • Collective. Every rank makes the same call. MPI_Bcast sends one value from a root to all. MPI_Scatter deals an array out in equal pieces and MPI_Gather collects them. MPI_Reduce combines one value from each rank into a single result at the root.

A typical program is: rank 0 reads the input, scatters it, every rank works on its piece, and a reduce or gather brings the answer back. Each rank works out which piece is its own with the block formula from the first lesson.

Inside, a reduce does not have every rank send to rank 0 in turn. The ranks pair up, then the survivors pair up, and so on: about log p rounds instead of p. One exercise has you produce that schedule.

MapReduce

MPI gives full control and expects you to handle everything, including a machine dying halfway through. MapReduce offers much less and handles the rest. You write two functions:

  • map takes one record and returns (key, value) pairs
  • reduce takes one key with all the values that were paired with it, and returns a result

Between them the framework does the shuffle: it gathers all pairs with the same key onto one machine. Counting words is the standard example. Map says ("the", 1) for each word; reduce adds up the ones.

Because a map call depends on nothing but its record, the framework can run it anywhere, and run it again somewhere else if a machine fails. That is the whole trick, and it is why the two functions must not keep any state between calls.

A combiner is a reduce that runs early, on each machine, on the pairs that machine produced, so that ("the", 1) five hundred times travels as ("the", 500) once. It is only safe when combining in pieces gives the same answer as combining all at once. Sums, minimums and maximums are safe. A mean is not: the mean of two means is not the mean of the whole. The cure is to carry a sum and a count, and divide at the very end.

Hadoop is the open implementation: files are cut into large blocks stored on several machines by HDFS, and the map runs on a machine that already holds the block. Spark keeps the same idea, holds the data in memory between steps, and lets you chain many maps and reduces, which suits the repeated passes of machine learning.

The same shape, again

Private partial results, combined at the end:

WherePartial resultCombined by
OpenMPeach thread's private totalthe reduction clause
GPUpairs of elementsrounds of a tree
MPIeach rank's valueMPI_Reduce
MapReduceeach machine's combined pairsthe reducer
Federated learningeach client's update and its sample countthe server's weighted average

The last row is where your research interest sits. Federated averaging is a map on every client and a reduce on the server, and weighting each client by its number of samples is the combiner done properly.

lessons.title: SQL: filter, group and join
lessons.html:
Every step of the ETL project reads or writes SQL. This lesson covers the part you use every day: pick rows, group them, and join tables. The examples use the same small bank as the exercises: customers, accounts (a customer can have several, or none) and transactions.

1. The order SQL really runs in

You write SELECT first, but the database runs the clauses in this order. Most beginner mistakes come from forgetting it.

  1. FROM and JOIN: which rows exist
  2. WHERE: keep some rows
  3. GROUP BY: put rows into groups
  4. HAVING: keep some groups
  5. SELECT: work out the columns
  6. ORDER BY, then LIMIT

That is why WHERE cannot use SUM(amount) (no groups exist yet) and why a column alias from SELECT usually cannot be used in WHERE.

2. Filter and sort

SELECT id, ts, amount, merchant
FROM transactions
WHERE kind = 'debit' AND amount > 5000
ORDER BY ts DESC, id;

ORDER BY ts DESC, id sorts newest first, and breaks ties by the lower id. Without a tie-breaker the order of equal rows is not guaranteed, and a report that changes between runs is a bug.

3. Group and aggregate

SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS n, SUM(amount) AS spent
FROM transactions
WHERE kind = 'debit'
GROUP BY category
HAVING SUM(amount) > 10000
ORDER BY spent DESC;

Every column in SELECT is either in GROUP BY or inside an aggregate (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX). WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after.

4. Buckets with CASE

SELECT id,
       CASE WHEN amount >= 10000 THEN 'large'
            WHEN amount >= 1000  THEN 'medium'
            ELSE 'small' END AS size
FROM transactions;

The first true branch wins, so put the most specific test first, just as with if and elif in Python.

5. NULL means "unknown"

  • city = NULL is never true. Write city IS NULL or city IS NOT NULL.
  • COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(city) skips NULLs. SUM and AVG skip them too.
  • COALESCE(city, 'unknown') swaps a NULL for a value you choose.

6. Joins

  • INNER JOIN: only pairs that match. A customer with no account disappears.
  • LEFT JOIN: every row on the left, with NULLs on the right where nothing matches.
  • Anti join: a left join, then keep the rows where the right side is NULL. This is how the ETL project finds orphans.
  • Self join: a table joined to itself under two aliases, for example two customers in the same city.
-- customers who have no account
SELECT c.id, c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.id
WHERE a.id IS NULL;

Put a condition on the right-hand table in ON, not WHERE, when you want to keep the unmatched rows. A WHERE on a right-hand column throws the NULL rows away and quietly turns your left join into an inner join.

7. A join can multiply rows

A customer with two accounts appears twice after JOIN accounts. Counting customers after that join needs COUNT(DISTINCT c.id). Joining two child tables of the same parent, such as order lines and payments, multiplies them together. Step 2 of the project calls this fan-out.

In the exercises

Type just the query. The practice page runs it for you. The 8 exercises follow this lesson's order, and Customers who never transacted is the checkpoint: solve it and this topic counts as known.

Say it out loud

Before you open the exercises, explain these in a sentence each: the difference between WHERE and HAVING, between an inner and a left join, and why = NULL never matches.

lessons.title: The pipeline and its contract
lessons.html:
A data pipeline moves data from where it is produced to where it is used, and makes it trustworthy on the way. This course follows one pipeline, the e-commerce ETL project, from raw files to a star schema, a dashboard, a scheduler and a stream. Each lesson is one step of the project.

The lifecycle

Every pipeline has the same stages: generate (a shop's database records orders), ingest (copy them out), store, transform (clean, join, model) and serve (tables, dashboards, models). Around them sit the undercurrents: security, data management, orchestration and quality. A data engineer is responsible for the whole line, not one tool on it.

Batch processes a bounded set at a time (yesterday's orders); streaming processes events as they arrive. ETL transforms before loading the warehouse; ELT loads raw data first and transforms inside it. This project does both: a batch path through Postgres and Spark, and a streaming path through Kafka.

The source

Olist is a real Brazilian marketplace: about 100,000 orders from 2016 to 2018, in nine CSV files. The project uses seven: customers, sellers, products, category translations, orders, order items and payments. Two facts about it shape everything later:

  • customer_id is new for every order. The person is customer_unique_id.
  • An order has several lines (order_items) and can have several payments, at two different grains.

A contract, then a profile

A data contract writes down what the source promises: tables, columns, types, which columns may be empty, accepted values, ranges, keys. In the project it is one Python file, contracts.py, and everything else is generated from it: the synthetic data, the profiler, the Spark rules and the quality checks. Change the contract and they all change together.

Profiling compares the data with the contract before anything is transformed: row counts, missing values, distinct values, ranges, keys that repeat, children without parents. Read every column as text when profiling. A reader that guesses types will turn the zip 01037 into 1037 and a price of 129,90 into a missing value, and you will never see either problem.

Data with known defects

Real data never tells you which rows are wrong, so you cannot measure your checks on it. The project therefore also generates Olist-shaped data with a seed, injects 14 kinds of defects at a chosen rate (exact duplicates, a missing customer, statuses in the wrong case or outside the accepted set, deliveries before purchase, timestamps after the extract, orphans, prices that are not positive, decimal commas and more) and writes the list to _defects.csv. That file is the ground truth the quality checks are scored against in step 5.

In the project

Step 1: STEP-01 data sources and profiling. Run python -m ecom_etl generate and python -m ecom_etl profile, then compare the profile with _manifest.json.

Read beside it

  • Fundamentals of Data Engineering (Reis and Housley, O'Reilly): ch. 2, The Data Engineering Lifecycle, and ch. 5, Data Generation in Source Systems.
  • LinkedIn Learning: Data Engineering Foundations, and Data Science Foundations: Data Engineering for staging and profiling.

lessons.title: Keys, grain and normal forms
lessons.html:
Before tables are loaded anywhere, decide what one row means and what identifies it. Most wrong numbers in analytics come from getting one of these two wrong.

Keys

  • A primary key identifies one row: order_id in orders, (order_id, order_item_id) in order items. It must be present and unique.
  • A foreign key points at another table's primary key: order_items.product_id points at products. A child whose parent does not exist is an orphan.
  • A natural key comes from the business (an order number). A surrogate key is made by the warehouse; step 4 needs one.

Grain

The grain is what one row stands for: one order, one order line, one payment, one day. Every number in a table must be true at its grain. Order lines and payments are both children of an order but at different grains, so joining them pairs every line with every payment. An order with two lines and one payment then counts its payment twice. This is fan-out, and the cure is always the same: bring each table to the grain you want, then join.

Normal forms

Normalisation removes repeated facts, so that each fact is stored once and cannot disagree with itself.

  • 1NF: one value per cell, no lists in a column, a key for every row.
  • 2NF: with a composite key, no column depends on only part of it. product_category depends on product_id, not on (order_id, item_no), so it leaves the order items table.
  • 3NF: no column depends on another non-key column. If zip determined city, city would move to a table keyed by zip.

The test for 3NF is a functional dependency: does one column's value fix another's? Check it in the data, not in your head. Real data often breaks the rule you expected, and then the column has to stay where it is.

Normalised tables (3NF) suit an application that writes: one update in one place. Analytics wants the opposite, few joins and wide rows, and step 4 deliberately denormalises into a star schema. Both are right for their job.

In the project

Step 2: STEP-02 Postgres landing zone and normalisation. The core schema is in 3NF, with primary keys, foreign keys and check constraints.

Read beside it

  • Fundamentals of Data Engineering: the data modelling part of ch. 8, Queries, Modeling, and Transformation.
  • Learning SQL, 3rd Ed. (Beaulieu, O'Reilly): constraints, joins and subqueries, if your SQL feels rusty.

lessons.title: Docker and Compose
lessons.html:
A pipeline has several moving parts: a database, the pipeline code with its Java and Python versions, a scheduler, a message broker, a dashboard. Docker packages each one with everything it needs, so it runs the same on your laptop, on a colleague's and in CI.

Images and containers

An image is a read-only file system plus a start command, built from a Dockerfile one layer per instruction. A container is a running image with its own processes, network and a thin writable layer that disappears with it. Data that must survive goes in a volume.

FROM python:3.11-slim-bookworm
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends openjdk-17-jre-headless
COPY . /opt/ecom
RUN pip install -e "/opt/ecom[spark,postgres]"
ENTRYPOINT ["python", "-m", "ecom_etl"]

Order the layers from least to most often changed: dependencies before source code, so editing a file does not reinstall everything.

Compose

docker-compose.yml declares the services, their images, ports, volumes, environment and health checks. docker compose up -d postgres starts one service; docker compose run --rm pipeline run runs a one-off command in another. Profiles keep optional services (Kafka, Airflow, pgAdmin) off unless asked for.

The detail that trips everyone once: inside a container, localhost is that container. Services reach each other by service name on the Compose network, so the pipeline connects to postgres:5432, while you, on the host, use the published port localhost:5432. Kafka needs two listeners for the same reason, one for containers and one for the host.

A health check tells Compose when a service is ready, not just started. depends_on with condition: service_healthy stops the pipeline from connecting to a database that is still initialising.

In the project

Steps 2, 8 and 9 add Postgres, Airflow and Kafka to docker-compose.yml, and CI builds the images and runs the whole pipeline inside them.

Read beside it

  • Docker's own Get started guide and the Compose file reference.
  • Data Engineering Zoomcamp, module 01-docker-terraform: Docker, Postgres and pgAdmin, the same setup as step 2.

lessons.title: Loading Postgres: raw, then core
lessons.html:
Loading is two jobs that are easier apart: get the bytes in without failing, then turn them into typed, constrained tables. The project uses two schemas for this, raw and core.

Raw: land everything as text

The raw tables have the source's columns, all of type text, plus a load id. Nothing is validated, so the load cannot fail on a bad value, and the raw schema is an exact, queryable copy of what arrived. Bulk loads use COPY, which streams a whole file in one command. One INSERT per row pays a network round trip and a parse for every row and is many times slower.

Core: types, keys and constraints

The core tables declare what the data must satisfy: types, NOT NULL, primary keys, foreign keys, CHECK constraints such as price >= 0 or delivered_at >= purchased_at. Building core from raw is SQL, in a fixed order:

  1. Deduplicate: one row per key, the first one loaded. In Postgres, SELECT DISTINCT ON (order_id) ... ORDER BY order_id, load_id.
  2. Standardise what is safe to fix: spaces, case, a decimal comma.
  3. Validate: pg_input_is_valid(value, 'timestamp') tests a cast without failing; accepted values, ranges, ordering of timestamps.
  4. Reject rows that fail, and their children: an order line whose order was rejected cannot be loaded either. The rejects are filtered out before the INSERT, because one bad row would otherwise abort the whole statement; comparing raw and core counts says how many went. (The Spark path of step 3 keeps every rejected row, with its reasons, in a quarantine.)
  5. Insert the survivors; the constraints are the last line of defence.

Deduplicate before validating. If you validate first, an invalid first copy lets a later copy through, and a rerun can pick a different row than last time.

Idempotent loads

A load you can run twice and get the same tables is idempotent. The project does it the simplest way: each load drops and rebuilds its tables inside one transaction, so a failure leaves the previous state intact. Retries, backfills and step 8's scheduler all depend on this.

In the project

Step 2: STEP-02, with load-raw and build-core in the CLI and the rules in sql/core.sql. The row counts of core match the Spark silver layer of step 3 exactly; that agreement is itself a test.

Read beside it

  • Fundamentals of Data Engineering: ch. 6, Storage, and ch. 7, Ingestion.
  • The Postgres manual: COPY, DISTINCT ON, pg_input_is_valid and the Constraints section of the DDL chapter.

lessons.title: Spark: DataFrames, laziness and the shuffle
lessons.html:
New to Spark? Start here. This lesson builds on two things you already know, Python and the SQL from the previous topic, and ends at the Spark code in your ETL repo.

1. Why Spark exists

pandas and SQLite run on one machine and want the data to fit in its memory. When the data is bigger than one machine, or the job is too slow on one core, you split the table into pieces and work on the pieces at the same time. Spark does that splitting, the scheduling and the recovery from failures for you. You write what looks like one table query, and Spark runs it on every core of your laptop or on a thousand machines, with the same code.

The Olist data in the ETL project would fit in pandas. The project uses Spark anyway because that is the tool data engineering jobs use for data that does not fit, and the habits (schemas, partitions, the shuffle) are what interviews ask about.

2. The picture: one boss, many workers

  • Your program runs on the driver, the boss that plans the work.
  • The table is cut into partitions, slices of rows. A file of a million orders might become 16 partitions.
  • Executors are the workers. Each takes one partition at a time and runs a task on it. On your laptop, local[*] means one worker thread per CPU core.

A DataFrame is Spark's table: named, typed columns, like a pandas DataFrame or a SQL table. The difference: a Spark DataFrame is a description of a distributed table, not the rows themselves.

3. Starting Spark

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql import functions as F   # F.col, F.date_format, F.count ...

spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("learn").master("local[*]").getOrCreate()
orders = spark.read.parquet("data/lake/synthetic/silver/orders")   # a cleaned copy of the orders
orders.printSchema()

data/lake/<source>/silver is where the project keeps the cleaned, typed tables; the next topic, Bronze, silver and quarantine, builds it. For now read it as "a clean orders table".

4. The same question, three ways

How many orders were delivered late, per purchase month? In the SQL you know:

SELECT substr(purchased_at, 1, 7) AS month, COUNT(*) AS late
FROM orders
WHERE delivered_at > estimated_at
GROUP BY month;

Spark runs that SQL as it is: orders.createOrReplaceTempView("orders"), then spark.sql("SELECT ..."). Or you write it with DataFrame methods, one method per clause:

late = (orders
        .filter(F.col("delivered_at") > F.col("estimated_at"))           # WHERE
        .groupBy(F.date_format("purchased_at", "yyyy-MM").alias("month"))  # GROUP BY
        .count())                                                        # COUNT(*)
late.show()

Both become the same plan. As in SQL, NULL > x is NULL, so orders not yet delivered drop out of the filter on their own.

5. Lazy: nothing runs until you ask for a result

Transformations (select, filter, withColumn, join, groupBy) only add a step to a plan and return a new DataFrame, instantly. Actions (show, count, collect, write) run the plan. In the code above, nothing touched the data until late.show().

Waiting pays off: Spark sees the whole plan before it starts, so its optimiser can read only the columns you use, push the filter down to the files and pick a join strategy. late.explain() prints the plan. Every action runs the plan again from the start; call .cache() on a DataFrame you reuse.

6. Narrow and wide: the shuffle

A narrow step works on each partition where it sits: filter, select, withColumn. No data moves.

A wide step needs all rows with the same key in one place: groupBy, join, distinct, window functions. To get there, every row is sent to partition hash(key) % n. That move is the shuffle: rows are written to disk, sent over the network and read back. It is the MapReduce shuffle from the scalable systems course, and it is where most of a job's time goes. In explain() it shows as Exchange.

7. Schemas, types and Parquet

  • Give Spark the schema instead of inferSchema: inference reads the file an extra time and guesses, so a zip code "01037" becomes the number 1037.
  • ANSI mode (the default in Spark 4): a bad cast such as "abc" to int stops the job with an error instead of quietly giving NULL. Cleaning code uses try_cast and try_to_timestamp, which return NULL on purpose so a rule can record why.
  • Parquet stores data column by column, compressed, with the schema and min/max values in each file. Reading 3 of 20 columns reads about 3/20 of the bytes, and a filter can skip whole files. partitionBy("_purchase_month") on write makes one folder per month, so a query for one month reads one folder.

8. Connect the dots: where each idea lives in your ETL repo

  • Driver, executors, the shuffle's n: src/ecom_etl/spark/session.py builds the one SparkSession with local[*] and sets spark.sql.shuffle.partitions to 16.
  • Explicit schema, Parquet, an action: bronze.py reads each CSV with an all-text schema from the contract, adds lineage columns, and only .write.parquet(...) makes it run.
  • Safe casts, a wide step, partitioned output: silver.py types columns with try_cast, keeps the first copy of a duplicate with Window.partitionBy(...) (a shuffle), and writes orders with partitionBy("_purchase_month").
  • The whole walkthrough: STEP-03: batch with PySpark, with a code tour and its own exercises.

9. Practise here, then on your laptop

The two exercises after this lesson run in the browser on a small imitation of Spark that has the same method names: Late deliveries, the lazy way (build a plan, see that nothing runs, find the shuffle) and The shuffle, by hand (send rows to hash(key) % n and count what moves). Two MapReduce exercises follow for the same idea one level lower.

Real PySpark needs Java 17. On Windows, run it in Docker or WSL, as STEP-03 explains:

pip install -e ".[dev,spark]"
python -m ecom_etl bronze --source synthetic
python -m ecom_etl silver --source synthetic

Then open a Python shell, read data/lake/synthetic/silver/orders, run the late-deliveries query from section 4, and find Exchange in late.explain(). That is this topic's outcome. The lesson shortens the column names; in the real table they are order_purchase_timestamp, order_delivered_customer_date and order_estimated_delivery_date.

Say it out loud

Before the exercises, explain in a sentence each: what a partition is; why orders.filter(...) returns instantly; which of filter, groupBy and join cause a shuffle, and why that is slow.

Read beside it

  • Learning Spark, 2nd Ed. (Damji et al., O'Reilly): ch. 1 to 4.
  • LinkedIn Learning: Apache Spark Essential Training: Big Data Engineering. Udemy: Taming Big Data with Apache Spark and Python (Frank Kane) for hands-on practice.
  • Data Engineering Zoomcamp, module 06-batch.

lessons.title: Bronze, silver and quarantine
lessons.html:
The lake has layers, each with one job. This is the medallion layout:

LayerHoldsRule
bronzethe source as received, as text, plus load metadatanever edited; the replayable record
silvertyped, cleaned, deduplicated rows that satisfy the contractone row per key; trusted
quarantinerows that failed, with every reasonnothing is dropped silently
goldthe star schema and aggregates for analysisstep 4

Silver, rule by rule

Each rule from the contract becomes one Spark expression that returns a reason code or NULL:

reasons = F.array_compact(F.array(
    F.when(F.col("customer_id").isNull(), F.lit("not_null:customer_id")),
    F.when(~F.col("status").isin(*ACCEPTED), F.lit("accepted_values:status")),
    F.when(F.col("purchased_at").isNull() & F.col("purchased_at_raw").isNotNull(), F.lit("type:purchased_at")),
    F.when(F.col("delivered_at") < F.col("purchased_at"), F.lit("sequence:delivered_before_purchase")),
))
silver     = df.filter(F.size(reasons) == 0)
quarantine = df.filter(F.size(reasons) > 0).withColumn("reasons", reasons)

Collecting all reasons, not the first, matters for the report: a row with two problems counts against two checks. Standardising (trim, lower case, a decimal comma) happens before the rules and is counted as a fix, not a rejection.

Duplicates and keys

An exact duplicate row is a harmless copy: drop it and count it. A key that reappears with different values is two versions of the truth: keep the first, quarantine the rest as duplicate_key. Spark's dropDuplicates handles the first case, and a window with row_number() the second.

Orphans and their children

A foreign key check is an anti join (join(parents, key, "left_anti")). The project separates two cases: a line whose order never existed is an orphan (fk:); a line whose order existed but was quarantined is parent_quarantined:. Only the first is a defect in the source, and mixing them would make the checks' precision look wrong in step 5.

In the project

Step 3: STEP-03, spark/silver.py. Silver's counts equal the Postgres core of step 2: two independent implementations of one contract agreeing.

Read beside it

  • Learning Spark, 2nd Ed.: ch. 3 and 4; ch. 9 on reliable data lakes.
  • Spark: The Definitive Guide (Chambers and Zaharia): the chapters on joins and data sources, as reference.

lessons.title: Star schema and slowly changing dimensions
lessons.html:
3NF suits the application that writes data. Analysis wants to filter, group and sum with few joins. Kimball's dimensional model is built for that: facts in the middle, dimensions around them, a star.

Facts and dimensions

  • A fact table records events at a declared grain, with numeric measures and keys to dimensions. fact_order_line: one row per order line, with price, freight and line total. fact_payment: one row per payment.
  • A dimension describes the who, what, where and when: dim_customer, dim_product, dim_seller, dim_date. Dimensions are wide and small; facts are narrow and large.

Every question then has the same shape: filter the fact, join the dimensions you slice by, group by their attributes.

Surrogate keys and the unknown member

Facts point at dimensions through surrogate keys made by the warehouse. The project derives them with xxhash64 of the natural key, so they are the same on every run and need no lookup table. Each dimension has an unknown member with key -1: a fact whose product is missing points there instead of vanishing from inner joins, so totals stay complete and the gap is visible.

Slowly changing dimensions

People move. What should an old order report as the customer's state?

  • Type 1 overwrites the attribute. Simple, and history is rewritten: last year's sales move to the new state.
  • Type 2 adds a new row per version, with effective_from, effective_to and is_current. The current version ends at a far-future date.
  • Type 3 keeps the previous value in an extra column. Rarely enough.

The project's dim_customer is Type 2. Versions come from the addresses seen on a person's orders, in time order: lag detects a change, a running sum of changes numbers the versions, and lead gives each version's end.

The point-in-time join

Building the fact, each order picks the version valid when it was placed:

effective_from <= purchased_at AND purchased_at < effective_to

The interval is half open, so the instant a new version starts belongs to it alone: no order matches two versions and none falls between them. The fact stores that version's surrogate key, and the join never has to be repeated.

In the project

Step 4: STEP-04 dimensional model, spark/gold.py, then load-gold into Postgres with constraints and indexes.

Read beside it

  • The Data Warehouse Toolkit, 3rd Ed. (Kimball and Ross): ch. 1 to 3, and ch. 5 for slowly changing dimensions. The retail sales case in ch. 3 is close to this project.
  • LinkedIn Learning: Introduction to Data Warehouses.
  • Data Engineering Zoomcamp, modules 03-data-warehouse and 04-analytics-engineering.

lessons.title: Data quality as code
lessons.html:
"The data looks fine" is not a test. A quality check is code that runs on every load, has a name, a severity and a threshold, and leaves a record.

Two kinds of checks

  • Row-level rules decide for one row: not null, accepted values, range, type, timestamp order, key present in the parent. The project generates 80 of them from the contract; they are what silver uses to quarantine.
  • Table-level gates look at a whole table: no duplicate keys, referential integrity of the fact to every dimension, row counts within bounds, freshness (the newest event is recent enough), the quarantine rate below a limit, reconciliations (gold revenue equals silver revenue; payments match items). The project has 35.

The common dimensions of quality are completeness, uniqueness, validity, consistency, accuracy and timeliness. Each check above tests one of them.

Gates and write-audit-publish

A blocking gate stops the run. The pattern is write, audit, publish: write the new tables, run the gates on them, and publish (load to Postgres, swap the table) only if they pass. Consumers never see a broken table, they see yesterday's good one. Warning-level checks are recorded but do not stop anything.

Measure the checks themselves

A check is a classifier, so it has error rates. With the generator's _defects.csv as ground truth:

  • recall: of the rows made bad, the share the checks caught;
  • precision: of the rows the checks rejected, the share that really were bad.

Rows rejected only because their parent was rejected are left out of precision: they are consequences, not detections. On 20,000 orders with 1% defects the project quarantines 3,497 rows (1,762 injected defects and their dependent rows) with precision and recall of 100%; on real Olist data there is no ground truth, which is exactly why the synthetic run exists.

History

Every run writes its results to a table: check, layer, rows checked, rows failed, passed, run id, time. A check that passes but whose failure count creeps up week by week is the early warning; the dashboard's data quality tab plots it.

In the project

Step 5: STEP-05 data quality framework, spark/quality.py and python -m ecom_etl quality.

Read beside it

  • Data Quality Fundamentals (Moses, Gavish and Vorwerck, O'Reilly): ch. 1 to 4.
  • Data Engineering Design Patterns (Konieczny, O'Reilly): the data quality chapter, for write-audit-publish and dead-letter patterns.
  • Data Engineering Zoomcamp, module 04: dbt tests are the same idea declared in YAML.

lessons.title: Analytics SQL and a dashboard
lessons.html:
The star schema exists to answer questions. Most business questions need the same few SQL patterns, and window functions are the one that separates a beginner from someone who can do the job.

CTEs

A WITH clause names an intermediate result. Write a hard query as a chain of small named steps: aggregate, then rank, then filter. Each step can be run and checked on its own.

Window functions

f(...) OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...) computes a value from related rows without collapsing them, as GROUP BY would.

  • ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK: the top N per group, the first event per key.
  • LAG, LEAD: the previous or next row: month over month growth, time between orders.
  • SUM(...) OVER (ORDER BY ...): running totals and cumulative shares, as in a Pareto cut.
  • SUM(...) OVER (): the grand total on every row, for percentages.

Two traps. A window's ORDER BY without a tie-breaker makes equal rows peers that share one running total. And LAG gives the previous row, which is not the previous month when a month has no data; join a calendar (dim_date) first.

Ten questions

The project answers ten: monthly revenue and growth, top categories with their share, revenue by state (where the customer lived when ordering, from the SCD Type 2 dimension), late deliveries by state, repeat customers, payment mix and installments, seller concentration (a Pareto cut), the weekday pattern, customers who moved, and RFM segments. Each is one file in sql/analysis/ with its expected shape tested in CI. Note how often the person key matters: repeat rate counted by customer_id is zero, because Olist issues a new one for every order.

A dashboard as code

The dashboard is a Streamlit app reading the gold tables in Postgres: sales, delivery, customers, streaming and data quality tabs. Being code, it is reviewed, versioned and tested like the rest (streamlit.testing.v1.AppTest renders every tab in CI). Cache the queries (st.cache_data with a time to live), and show where each number comes from and how fresh it is.

lessons.title: Making it fast: Spark and Postgres tuning
lessons.html:
Tuning is measurement first. Record a baseline, change one thing, measure again, keep what helps. The project's benchmark does exactly this on 201,874 orders on a 4-core runner:

ConfigurationSilver + goldSpeed-up
baseline: 200 shuffle partitions, no broadcasts, AQE off176.9 s1.0x
+ shuffle partitions sized to the machine (8)39.5 s4.5x
+ broadcast joins for the dimensions33.0 s5.4x
+ adaptive query execution33.6 s5.3x

Shuffle partitions

spark.sql.shuffle.partitions (default 200) is how many partitions every shuffle produces. On a small cluster and modest data, 200 means hundreds of tiny tasks whose scheduling costs more than their work. On huge data, too few means tasks that spill to disk. Aim for partitions of roughly 100 to 200 MB, and at least as many as cores.

Join strategies

A sort-merge join shuffles and sorts both sides. A broadcast hash join copies the small side to every executor and never shuffles the large one. A star schema is made for broadcasts: one big fact, small dimensions. Spark broadcasts automatically below spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold (10 MB), and F.broadcast(dim) forces it.

Skew

A stage is as slow as its slowest task. When one key holds far more rows (the best-selling product), its partition becomes a straggler, visible in the Spark UI as one task far above the median. Remedies: broadcast so the key is never shuffled, let AQE split skewed partitions at run time, or salt the hot key. AQE also merges small partitions and can switch a join to a broadcast once it knows real sizes; it gained nothing here because the first two changes had already removed its work.

Layout and pruning

Partitioning the fact by month lets a query for one month read one folder: 1.0 MB scanned instead of 15.8 MB. At this size the time barely changes; at terabytes it decides everything. Avoid partitioning by a column with thousands of values: millions of small files are slower than none.

Postgres: indexes and plans

EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows the plan and the real time. A Seq Scan on a selective filter usually means a missing index. Postgres indexes primary keys automatically and foreign keys never; adding indexes on the fact's keys took one customer's order history from 12.5 ms to 0.013 ms. Each index slows writes and takes space, so index what you filter and join on.

In the project

Read beside it

lessons.title: Orchestration with Airflow
lessons.html:
A pipeline that only runs when you type the commands is a script. An orchestrator runs the steps in order on a schedule, retries what failed, records what happened and lets you rerun a past day.

DAGs and tasks

In Airflow a pipeline is a DAG, a directed acyclic graph of tasks. An edge means "runs after". Acyclic is what makes an order possible at all: the scheduler repeatedly runs the tasks whose upstream tasks have all succeeded, which is a topological sort.

from airflow.sdk import DAG
from airflow.providers.standard.operators.bash import BashOperator

with DAG("ecom_batch_pipeline", schedule="@daily", catchup=False, max_active_runs=1,
         default_args={"retries": 2}) as dag:
    steps = [BashOperator(task_id=name, bash_command=f"{CLI} {name}") for name in
             ["bronze", "silver", "silver_gate", "gold", "gold_gate", "load_gold", "analyze"]]
    for up, down in zip(steps, steps[1:]):
        up >> down

Runs, retries and backfills

  • Each scheduled run has a logical date: the period it processes, not the moment it runs.
  • Retries rerun a failed task after a delay; good for a database that was briefly unreachable. The project's quality gates have retries=0: bad data does not improve by waiting.
  • A backfill runs the DAG for past dates; catchup decides whether missed intervals run automatically.
  • Params let a manual run choose its input, here the source (synthetic or Olist) and the number of orders.

Idempotent tasks

Retries and backfills run tasks again, so every task must give the same result when run twice: overwrite the run's output rather than append, upsert rather than insert. If a task is not idempotent, the orchestrator's main features become ways to corrupt data.

Gates in the DAG

Making silver_gate and gold_gate separate tasks puts write-audit-publish in the graph. When a gate fails, every task downstream is marked "upstream failed" and nothing is published, and the UI shows exactly which check stopped the run.

Testing a DAG

A DAG is code and is tested like code: it imports without errors, has the expected tasks and edges, and airflow dags test runs it once end to end, which the project's CI does on every push.

In the project

Step 8: STEP-08 orchestration with Airflow, airflow/dags/ecom_pipeline.py, and docker compose --profile airflow up.

Read beside it

  • Data Pipelines Pocket Reference (Densmore, O'Reilly): orchestration and DAG design.
  • LinkedIn Learning: Hands-On Introduction: Data Engineering. Udemy: The Complete Hands-On Introduction to Apache Airflow (Marc Lamberti); pick a version that covers Airflow 3.

lessons.title: Streaming: Kafka and Structured Streaming
lessons.html:
Batch asks "what happened yesterday". Streaming keeps the answer current as events arrive. The ideas that make it correct (event time, watermarks, idempotent sinks) are the same in every streaming system.

Kafka

Kafka is a distributed, append-only log. Producers write messages (key, value, timestamp) to a topic, which is split into partitions. Each message gets an offset, its position in its partition. Consumers read at their own pace and record their offsets; messages stay for a retention period whether read or not, so a consumer can replay.

  • The partition is chosen from a hash of the key, so all messages with one key go to one partition, and order is guaranteed only within a partition. The project keys order events by order_id.
  • Partitions are the unit of parallelism: more partitions, more consumers in parallel.
  • Delivery is at least once by default: after a crash a consumer rereads from its last committed offset, and a producer that retries can write a message twice.

Event time and watermarks

Event time is when something happened; processing time is when you saw it. Daily revenue must use event time, or a network delay moves sales to the wrong day. Events arrive out of order, so how long do you wait for a late one? A watermark says: once the newest event time seen is T, nothing older than T minus the delay is expected. Windows older than that are final, their state is dropped, and later data for them is discarded and counted. A long delay accepts more stragglers and keeps more state; a short one is faster and drops more.

Structured Streaming

Spark treats a stream as a table that keeps growing and runs the same DataFrame code on each micro-batch. The project's stream has four queries: bronze keeps every message; quarantine catches malformed JSON; silver parses, then dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark("event_id") with a 7-day watermark; and daily revenue groups by a one-day event-time window with a 3-day watermark.

Exactly-once results

From at-least-once input you get exactly-once results with three things together:

  1. a checkpoint per query, storing offsets and state, so a restart continues where it stopped;
  2. deduplication by a business key (event_id);
  3. an idempotent sink: foreachBatch upserts one row per window into Postgres, so writing a batch twice gives the same table.

In CI, 3,063 messages (with 63 duplicates, 34 late and 32 malformed) become 3,063 bronze rows, 32 quarantined and 2,968 silver events, and daily revenue in Postgres equals the producer's own total to the cent. The availableNow trigger processes everything available and stops, which suits tests and scheduled runs; a processing-time trigger runs for ever.

In the project

Read beside it

  • Kafka: The Definitive Guide, 2nd Ed. (Shapira et al., O'Reilly): producers, consumers, partitions and delivery semantics.
  • Learning Spark, 2nd Ed.: ch. 8, Structured Streaming. Streaming Systems (Akidau et al., O'Reilly) for event time and watermarks in depth.
  • LinkedIn Learning: Apache Kafka Essential Training: Getting Started. Data Engineering Zoomcamp, module 07-streaming.

lessons.title: Cloud platforms, and telling the story
lessons.html:
The pipeline runs on a laptop and in CI. The last step shows it is not tied to either, and turns the work into something you can explain in fifteen minutes.

Databricks

Databricks is managed Spark with notebooks, jobs and tables. Because the project's transformations are plain functions that take a Spark session and a lake location, the same silver and gold code runs there; only the entry point and the storage change (Unity Catalog volumes and tables instead of local folders). The Free Edition is enough to run the job on a sample and see the Spark UI on a real cluster.

Snowflake

Snowflake is a cloud warehouse that separates storage from compute: data sits in tables, and you pay for virtual warehouses only while they run queries. Loading the gold tables is the usual pattern: files to a stage, then COPY INTO a table, then the same analysis SQL with small dialect changes. A trial account is enough.

What changes in the cloud

  • Credentials live in a secret store or environment variables, never in the repository.
  • Cost becomes a design input: auto-suspend warehouses, size clusters to the job, prune partitions.
  • Storage is object storage, so files are immutable: table formats such as Delta Lake and Iceberg add transactions, schema evolution and time travel on top of Parquet.

The numbers, and where they came from

Every number on the resume comes from RESULTS.md, with the data, command, machine and date beside it: records ingested into the star schema, the 115 automated checks, the rows flagged per run, the runtime tuned from 176.9 s to 33.0 s. Say the conditions with the number. "On 201,874 synthetic orders on a 4-core CI runner" is a claim you can defend; "5x faster" alone is not.

The story

For each step, have one short story ready: the problem, the decision, what you measured, what you would do differently. STORIES.md in the repository has one per step. Good ones in this project: why bad rows go to quarantine instead of being dropped, why the customer dimension is Type 2, why the gates have no retries, and why exactly-once results need three mechanisms and not one.

In the project

Read beside it

  • The Databricks Free Edition documentation: notebooks, jobs and volumes.
  • Fundamentals of Data Engineering: ch. 3, Designing Good Data Architecture, and ch. 4, Choosing Technologies.

lessons.title: Chunking documents for retrieval
lessons.html:
Retrieval can only return what chunking produced, so this is the first quality lever. src/chunking.py has no dependencies on purpose: it is pure text processing, so it is tested anywhere.

The algorithm

  1. Split the document into paragraphs on blank lines.
  2. A paragraph longer than chunk_size (800 characters) is split into sentences.
  3. Pack units greedily into a buffer; when the next one would overflow, flush the buffer as a chunk and start the next buffer with the last overlap (120) characters of the flushed one.
candidate = f"{buffer}\n\n{unit}" if buffer else unit
if len(candidate) <= chunk_size or not buffer:
    buffer = candidate
else:
    chunks.append(buffer)
    tail = buffer[-overlap:] if overlap else ""
    buffer = f"{tail}\n\n{unit}" if tail else unit

Trade-offs to say out loud

  • Characters, not tokens. No tokenizer dependency; at about 4 characters per token the two track closely for English prose. Token chunking is more precise near context limits.
  • Natural boundaries. A half sentence embeds badly and gives the model a broken thought.
  • Overlap keeps a fact on a boundary findable from both chunks, at the cost of some duplicate text.

Every chunk keeps source and chunk_index: citations later depend on it.

lessons.title: Cosine similarity and exact vector search
lessons.html:
src/vectorstore.py is a hand-rolled store: four methods (add, query, save, load) over a NumPy matrix.

Normalise once, then cosine is a dot product

norms = np.linalg.norm(vectors, axis=1, keepdims=True)
norms[norms == 0] = 1.0          # a zero vector would divide by zero
vectors = vectors / norms

With unit rows and a unit query, scores = self._vectors @ q gives every chunk's cosine similarity in one matrix-vector product.

Top k without sorting everything

top_idx = np.argpartition(-scores, k - 1)[:k]        # O(n): the k best, unordered
top_idx = top_idx[np.argsort(-scores[top_idx])]     # sort only those k

Why not Chroma or FAISS?

For thousands of chunks brute force is exact nearest-neighbour search, answers in milliseconds and needs no service. It is O(n) per query. At hundreds of thousands to millions of vectors you switch to an approximate index (HNSW, IVF) that trades a little recall for sub-linear time. The narrow interface means that swap would not touch rag_chain.py or the agent.

lessons.title: Grounded answers with citations
lessons.html:
src/rag_chain.py is the RAG step itself: embed the question, retrieve the top k chunks, build a prompt, call the model, return the answer with its sources.

The prompt is the main defence

Chunks are numbered with their source:

[1] (source: ieee1722_avtp_communication.md)
...chunk text...
[2] (source: autosar_adaptive_overview.md)

The system prompt has four rules: answer only from the chunks, put a citation like [1] after every claim, say plainly when the context is not enough, be concise. With no chunks at all, the user message itself tells the model to say it cannot answer.

What it does not guarantee

A prompt lowers hallucination; it does not prevent it. Only a check of the answer against its sources (a verifier or critic step, or an LLM-as-judge evaluation) catches a claim the chunks do not support. Say that in an interview before you are asked.

Sources in citation order

RagAnswer.sources keeps each source file once, in retrieval order, so a UI can list them under the answer.

lessons.title: A ReAct agent loop with safe tools
lessons.html:
src/agent.py makes visible what LangChain's AgentExecutor hides. An agent is four things:

  1. a system prompt listing the tools and an exact reply format (Thought / Action / Action Input or Thought / Final Answer);
  2. a loop of at most max_steps (4) calls to the model;
  3. regex parsers for the action and the final answer;
  4. code that runs the chosen tool and appends Observation: ... to the transcript.

Two tools, so routing is visible

search_knowledge_base calls the RAG retriever; calculator evaluates arithmetic. "What is 1722 * 2 + 8?" should go to the calculator, not to a document search.

Model output never runs as code

tree = ast.parse(expression, mode="eval")
result = _safe_eval(tree.body)   # numbers and + - * / ** only

Anything else (names, calls, attributes) raises, and the error becomes the observation. Calling eval on model text would be remote code execution.

The same agent built with LangChain (agent_langchain.py) is what you demo when asked for LangChain; the hand-rolled one is what the tests cover, with a scripted fake model.

lessons.title: Retrieval evaluation: hit rate and MRR
lessons.html:
If retrieval misses, no prompt saves the answer, so retrieval gets numbers first. eval/eval_questions.json has 12 questions, each labelled with the document that should come back.

  • hit_rate@k: the share of questions whose expected document appears in the top k chunks.
  • MRR@k: the mean of 1/rank of the first chunk from the expected document (0 if absent). It rewards ranking the right document first.
rank = next((i for i, s in enumerate(sources, 1) if s == expected), None)
reciprocal_ranks.append(1.0 / rank if rank else 0.0)

Reading 1.00 honestly

Even TF-IDF reaches hit_rate@3 = 1.00 here: six short, topically distinct documents are easy for keyword overlap. That is a finding, not a failure: TF-IDF is a strong baseline on small distinct corpora. Dense embeddings earn their cost on paraphrases, synonyms and large overlapping corpora, which this set does not test. Twelve questions also cannot separate two good backends. The next step is a larger set with paraphrased questions, then answer-level checks.

lessons.title: Pluggable backends, FastAPI and zero-cost tests
lessons.html:
Every layer has a real and an offline implementation, chosen by configuration (src/config.py, .env):

LayerRealOffline
Embeddingssentence-transformers all-MiniLM-L6-v2TF-IDF (scikit-learn)
LLMOpenAI or Anthropica deterministic mock

So the tests check the pipeline's logic (chunking, the store, prompt building, agent routing) with no key, network, GPU or download, and the suite costs nothing to run in CI. Swapping a model changes a setting, not code.

Serving

src/api.py exposes GET /health and POST /query with {"question": ..., "mode": "rag" | "agent"}. Build the index once with scripts/build_index.py; the API loads it at start-up, not per request.

What is not tested, and why

The LangChain agent is left out of the suite: it needs LangChain and a real model. Say that, and say how you would test it (record and replay model responses).

lessons.title: The RAG assistant, explained
lessons.html:
Use this as the outline of your interview story.

  1. Problem. Engineers need answers from in-vehicle systems documents (AUTOSAR Adaptive, IEEE1722/AVTP, hypervisor bring-up, ROS2-cloud bridge) with sources they can check.
  2. Design. Paragraph-aware chunks; exact cosine search over a NumPy matrix; a grounding prompt with numbered citations; two agents (hand-rolled ReAct, tested; LangChain, demoed); FastAPI.
  3. Evidence. hit_rate@3 = 1.00 and MRR@3 = 1.00 on 12 labelled questions, and a test suite that runs offline at zero API cost.
  4. Limits. A small, keyword-friendly question set; no answer-level evaluation; brute-force search.
  5. Next. Paraphrased questions, hybrid BM25 plus dense retrieval with reranking, an answer faithfulness check, an ANN index if the corpus grows.

Why this corpus: it is your own engineering domain, so you can judge every answer yourself.

lessons.title: FedAvg: averaging models, not data
lessons.html:
Federated learning trains one model over data that never leaves its owner. Each round:

  1. the server sends the global weights to the selected clients;
  2. each client loads them, trains a few local epochs on its own data (3 in this testbed, Adam, cross-entropy) and returns the new weights and its sample count;
  3. the server averages the client weights, weighted by sample count, into the next global model.
w_global = Σ_k (n_k / n) · w_k

The same weighting is applied to metrics in server/fl_server.py:

losses = [m.get("train_loss", 0) * n for n, m in metrics]
agg = sum(losses) / total

Weighting by examples makes FedAvg approximate training on the union of the data; an unweighted mean would let a client with 50 samples move the model as much as one with 5,000.

The model here is a small MLP: 12 features → 32 → 16 → 3 classes.

lessons.title: A Flower server and NumPy clients
lessons.html:
The server

AggregationStrategy subclasses Flower's FedAvg and overrides aggregate_fit and aggregate_evaluate to log each client's samples and metrics before calling the parent. Settings: 5 rounds, min_fit_clients = min_evaluate_clients = min_available_clients = MIN_CLIENTS (2, or 3 with the Pi), and on_fit_config_fn sends the round number and local_epochs to clients.

A client

class VehicleClient(fl.client.NumPyClient):
    def get_parameters(self, config): return [p.detach().numpy() for p in self.model.parameters()]
    def fit(self, parameters, config):
        # load global weights, train 3 epochs
        return self.get_parameters(config), 300, {}
    def evaluate(self, parameters, config): ...

fit returns weights, the number of examples (the FedAvg weight) and a metrics dict. Returning {} means the server's weighted train_loss has nothing to average from that client: return {"train_loss": loss.item()} so the log means something.

Flower 1.x prefers the flower-supernode and ServerApp/ClientApp style; the testbed uses start_server and start_numpy_client, which still work but are deprecated. Know both.

lessons.title: gRPC between the server and the fleet
lessons.html:
Flower's transport is gRPC: one long-lived HTTP/2 connection per client, binary protobuf messages, streaming in both directions. Clients dial fl-server:8080 (the Compose service name); the server listens on 0.0.0.0:8080.

Why it fits

  • Weights are large float arrays sent every round: protobuf carries them as bytes; JSON would base64-inflate them by a third.
  • The connection stays open between rounds, so there is no reconnect per message.
  • Typed messages catch mismatches early.

This is the same reasoning as the KPIT edge-to-cloud telemetry bridge: high-rate binary data from edge devices over gRPC.

Failures are normal

aggregate_fit receives results and failures. A vehicle that drops mid-round lands in failures; the round still aggregates the others if at least min_fit_clients answered. Log failures; a fleet is never fully online.

lessons.title: A heterogeneous fleet with Docker Compose
lessons.html:
docker-compose.yml defines one bridge network, fl-net, and three services:

  • fl-server, publishing port 8080;
  • vehicle-ros2, a ROS2 image with ROS_DOMAIN_ID=10;
  • vehicle-lite, a plain Python client.

Both vehicles depends_on the server, which orders start-up but does not wait for readiness: a client may need to retry its first connection.

The Raspberry Pi

The third client runs bare-metal on aarch64. That changes three things: Python wheels must exist for arm64 (rpi_requirements.txt, extract_wheels.sh); it reaches the server by the host's LAN address, not the service name; and it trains slowest, so every synchronous round waits for it. Start the server with MIN_CLIENTS=3 when it joins.

Scripts: build_all.sh, run_all.sh, log_all.sh, rebuild_all.sh.

lessons.title: From ROS2 topics to training features
lessons.html:
client/fl_client_ros2.py turns live vehicle topics into training data.

class SensorBuffer:
    def add(self, speed, brake):
        with self.lock:
            self.speed.append(speed); self.brake.append(brake)
            if len(self.speed) > 300: self.speed.pop(0); self.brake.pop(0)

A ROS2 subscriber thread adds samples; the Flower thread reads them. The lock stops a read from seeing a half-updated pair of lists. Only the last 300 samples are kept, a sliding window.

Features

get_features stacks speed, brake and derived signals such as acceleration (np.gradient(speed)) into 12 features per sample, matching the MLP's input.

The fallback

If ROS2 is not installed (ROS2_AVAILABLE = False) or fewer than 10 samples have arrived, the client trains on torch.randn. That keeps a round alive, but random data adds noise to the global model. Log it, count it per round, and exclude such clients from evaluation.

lessons.title: Non-IID clients and honest evaluation
lessons.html:
Vehicles do not see the same data: one drives in the city, one on the highway. Data that is not independent and identically distributed (non-IID) makes local models drift in different directions; FedAvg then converges more slowly and can favour the largest client.

Remedies to know

  • Fewer local epochs or a smaller learning rate, so clients drift less per round.
  • FedProx: a penalty that keeps local weights close to the global ones.
  • Reporting per-client accuracy beside the global one.

The testbed's evaluation today

The lite client's evaluate returns 0.0, 100, {"accuracy": 0.5} every round, and training data is synthetic until ROS2 data arrives. The weighted accuracy on the server therefore cannot show learning. Fix it before quoting numbers:

  1. hold out 20% of each client's real data;
  2. return the true loss and accuracy on it;
  3. compare with a centralised model trained on the pooled data.

Saying this yourself in a review is a strength: it shows you know what the numbers mean.

lessons.title: The federated testbed, explained
lessons.html:
1. Problem. Vehicles generate data that should not leave them; can a fleet train one model anyway, across very different hardware?
  2. Design. Flower FedAvg over gRPC; a server that logs each round; a ROS2 vehicle, a lite container and a bare-metal Raspberry Pi (x86-64 and aarch64); shared feature extraction from speed and brake topics.
  3. Engineering. Docker Compose for the containers, arm64 wheels for the Pi, a thread-safe sensor buffer, MIN_CLIENTS to admit the third client.
  4. Honest status. Training falls back to synthetic data without ROS2 input, and one client reports a fixed accuracy, so today it demonstrates the system, not model quality.
  5. Next. Real held-out evaluation per client, non-IID splits, FedProx, a centralised baseline, round-time measurements with and without the Pi.

This is also the through-line from automotive work (ECUs, ROS2, gRPC telemetry) to federated learning research.

lessons.title: A leak-free scikit-learn pipeline
lessons.html:
src/cpu_baseline.py builds the UCI heart-disease model.

  • Target: y = (df['num'] > 0), disease present or not.
  • Numeric features (age, trestbps, chol, thalch, oldpeak, ca): median imputation, then standard scaling.
  • Categorical features (sex, cp, fbs, restecg, exang, slope, thal): most-frequent imputation, then one-hot encoding with handle_unknown='ignore'.
clf = Pipeline([('preprocess', preprocessor), ('model', LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))])
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=42)

Why everything sits inside the Pipeline

The imputer's medians and the scaler's means are learned from the data. Fitted on all rows, they leak the test set into training and inflate the score. Inside the Pipeline they are fitted on the training split only, and the same object is reused in cross-validation for each fold.

stratify=y keeps the disease rate the same in train and test.

lessons.title: Stratified CV, precision, recall and F1
lessons.html:
One train/test split of a few hundred rows gives a noisy number. Five stratified folds give five, each with the same disease rate; report the mean and the spread.

Which metric

  • Recall = TP / (TP + FN): of the patients with disease, how many the model flags. A missed patient is the costly error in screening.
  • Precision = TP / (TP + FP): of the flagged, how many are ill. Low precision means many false alarms.
  • F1: their harmonic mean, high only when both are.
  • Accuracy hides the balance between the two error types.

Logistic regression outputs probabilities; the default threshold 0.5 is a choice. Lowering it raises recall at the cost of precision. Pick it from the cross-validated precision-recall curve, never from the test set.

lessons.title: RAPIDS cuML: the same API on the GPU
lessons.html:
cuML reimplements scikit-learn's estimators on CUDA with the same interface:

from cuml.linear_model import LogisticRegression as cuLR
from cuml.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier as cuRF
lr_gpu = cuLR(max_iter=1000).fit(X_train, y_train)

src/export_preprocessed.py runs the scikit-learn preprocessing once and saves X_train.npy, X_test.npy, y_train.npy, y_test.npy under data/cuda/. Every CPU and GPU script then loads the same arrays, so a difference in time or accuracy comes from the estimator and hardware, not from preprocessing.

What does not carry over

  • Not every scikit-learn option exists in cuML; check the solver and parameters.
  • Random forests split differently, so accuracies agree closely, not exactly.
  • Metrics are computed with scikit-learn on the host, which is fine for a few hundred predictions.

Kaggle and the college V100 both run RAPIDS; the Dockerfile pins the environment.

lessons.title: Logistic regression as CUDA kernels
lessons.html:
src/cuda_logreg/ trains logistic regression without any library: four kernels in kernel.cu, a training loop in host.cu.

  1. logistic_forward: one thread per sample, pred[i] = sigmoid(X_i · w).
  2. compute_error: err[i] = pred[i] − y[i].
  3. compute_gradient: one thread per weight, grad[j] = (1/n) Σ_i err[i] · X[i][j].
  4. sgd_update: w[j] −= lr · grad[j].

That is gradient descent on the log loss, whose gradient is

∇w L = (1/n) · Xᵀ (σ(Xw) − y)

Host side

Copy X and y to the GPU once, then launch the four kernels per epoch with <<<numBlocks, blockSize>>>; copy only the final weights back. Copying every epoch would cost more than the arithmetic.

Check it: the learned weights should be close to scikit-learn's with the same preprocessing and no regularisation (penalty=None).

lessons.title: Measuring speedup honestly
lessons.html:
src/ma721_real_speedup.py shows both sides:

  • 200 trees on a few hundred rows: the GPU is slower. Transfers, kernel launches and cuML start-up outweigh tiny work.
  • 10,000 trees: the work dominates and the GPU wins.

Amdahl's law

S(N) = 1 / ((1 − p) + p / N)        →   1 / (1 − p) as N → ∞

If 80% of a run parallelises (p = 0.8), no GPU gives more than 5×. Data loading, preprocessing on the CPU and host-device copies are part of the serial share.

Timing rules

  1. Warm up once (the first GPU call includes initialisation).
  2. Repeat and report the median.
  3. Same data, same model size, same accuracy check.
  4. State the machine and data size next to the number.

So the resume says "up to 5×", and the interview answer explains when it is 1× or less.

lessons.title: The GPU pipeline, explained
lessons.html:
1. Problem. Predict heart disease from 13 clinical features, and find out when GPUs speed up classical ML.
  2. Baseline. A leak-free scikit-learn pipeline, stratified split, precision, recall and F1.
  3. Acceleration. The same arrays on RAPIDS cuML (logistic regression, random forest), and logistic regression written as four CUDA kernels.
  4. Result. Up to 5× faster training at large model sizes; slower than the CPU on small models, explained by overhead and Amdahl's law.
  5. Next. Clean up the exploratory scripts into one benchmark with repeats, add a threshold chosen for recall, and record times per machine.
